briefOverview: This chapter interweaves notices of key Israelite patriarchs dying in Egypt with geopolitical conflicts among Edom, Moab, and Midian. It emphasizes shifting alliances, tribute, and long-term enmity generated by wartime betrayal.
summary:
The chapter records the deaths of several sons of Jacob in Egypt—Reuben, Dan, Issachar, Asher, Gad, Judah, and Naphtali—each described with age, placement in a coffin, and being entrusted to their children.

In Edom, King Hadad son of Bedad campaigns against Moab with a vast force; Moab seeks Midianite help but then retreats mid-battle, leaving Midian to be destroyed, after which Moab becomes tributary to Hadad.

Surviving Midianites, joined by “children of the east” and “children of Keturah,” attempt revenge against Moab; Moab again appeals to Hadad, who defeats Midian and their allies and drives them back with heavy losses.

The narrative closes by highlighting enduring hostility and mutual violence between Midian and Moab along their roads, and by noting a later conflict in which Zepho son of Eliphaz (associated with Esau’s line) defeats raiders from Africa, causing Africa’s king to fear him thereafter.
externalContext:
The Book of Jasher is a later Jewish work that retells and expands biblical narratives; it is not part of the Hebrew Bible’s canon and survives in multiple forms, including a well-known 19th-century English edition.

“Hadad son of Bedad” appears as an Edomite king in biblical genealogical material (Genesis 36), reflecting a tradition of early Edomite monarchs. Moab and Midian are portrayed in the wider biblical world as neighboring peoples east/southeast of the Jordan with frequent interaction—sometimes conflict, sometimes temporary alliance.

The repeated mention of coffins and embalming aligns with an Egyptian setting as portrayed in Genesis, where elite burial practices and embalming are prominent in the narrative world of Israel’s sojourn in Egypt.
externalReferences:
The burial notices resemble the Genesis account of Jacob and Joseph being embalmed in Egypt and placed in a coffin (Genesis 50:2–3, 26), which provides a narrative backdrop for why such practices are mentioned for Jacob’s sons here.

The Edomite king “Hadad son of Bedad” is named in the Edom king list (Genesis 36:31–39; cf. 1 Chronicles 1:43–50), and Jasher’s account appears to expand this brief biblical reference into extended military campaigns.

The “children of Keturah” language echoes the biblical identification of Keturah’s descendants as eastern peoples (Genesis 25:1–6), here depicted as coming to Midian’s aid.
practicalQuestions: What does the repeated emphasis on burial practices and being “given into the hands of” children suggest about family responsibility across generations?
How do Moab’s choices in battle (seeking help, then retreating) illustrate the long-term costs of expedient decisions?
Where do I see cycles of retaliation in my context, and what would it take to interrupt them rather than perpetuate them?
How does the chapter portray political protection (Moab appealing to Hadad) as both a rescue and a form of subjugation (tribute)?
uncertainAreas: Some chronological markers (e.g., “fiftieth year” of Hadad’s reign versus earlier stated 35 years) appear internally inconsistent, and the identities/locations of “Chittim” and “Africa” in this retelling are not fully clear from the text alone, so I avoided over-identifying them.
